stages.title: Atoms & Bonds
stages.subtitle: Stage 1 — the gen-chem you are assumed to still have
stages.why: Orgo does not reteach any of this. It opens by assuming you can already say how many bonds an atom makes, which atom in a bond is electron-poor, and what a molecule looks like in three dimensions. Everything after this stage leans on it.

stages.title: Reading Organic Structures
stages.subtitle: Stage 2 — the notation the whole course is written in
stages.why: From week one, lectures are drawn in line-angle structures with the carbons and hydrogens invisible. If decoding a drawing takes conscious effort, you spend your attention on notation instead of chemistry. This stage is mostly repetition, and it pays off more than any other.

stages.title: How Reactions Work
stages.subtitle: Stage 3 — the reasoning engine
stages.why: These four are what orgo actually tests. Almost every mechanism opens or closes with a proton transfer, is drawn with curved arrows, is explained by delocalization, and is argued over with energy diagrams. Get here and lecture becomes a second exposure rather than a first.

stages.title: What's Coming
stages.subtitle: Stage 4 — a look down the road
stages.why: Not prerequisites — a preview, so the first weeks of lecture feel familiar rather than sudden.

roadmap.note: Most courses open with a fast review that assumes you already know it. This is the part rusty students most often underestimate.
Taught early precisely because every later mechanism uses it. pKa reasoning and resonance stability are the whole content.
Newman projections and chair conformations get added on top of the naming and isomer ideas you already have.
Chirality, R/S assignment, enantiomers and diastereomers. Builds directly on stereocenters and 3-D geometry.
The first big mechanism unit. Rate laws, leaving-group ability and carbocation stability all come from Stage 3.
Taught alongside substitution because they compete. Anti-periplanar geometry and the entropy argument for heat both appear here.
Markovnikov selectivity, carbocation rearrangements, and pi bonds acting as nucleophiles.
Radicals introduce fishhook arrows and bond dissociation energies.
IR and NMR arrive here in most courses. Functional-group recognition is what makes spectra readable.
